title: Simulate It, Understand It: A Practical Guide to Modelling with SimLab
author: Michael Borck

courses.title: Simulate It, Understand It: A Practical Guide to Modelling with SimLab
courses.pitch: Turn a system question into a reproducible, validated simulation.

unit.title: Simulate It, Understand It: A Practical Guide to Modelling with SimLab
unit.pitch: Turn a system question into a reproducible, validated simulation.

blocks.html: A simulation is not a prediction. It is a question about a system, made runnable.

A simulation is a model with time. It represents the parts of a system that matter for a question, the rules that connect them, and the way state changes.

The question comes first. "What happens if demand doubles?" is a simulation question. "Build a stock market model" is not. The first names a change and an outcome. The second names a tool.

A useful simulation brief states:

  • the system and the boundary
  • the question
  • the parts that matter
  • the rules
  • the time horizon
  • the output that answers the question
  • the assumption that would change the answer

A simulation is always a simplification. The skill is choosing the simplification that preserves the answer.

A wind tunnel is not the aeroplane. It is a controlled model of the air and the surfaces that matter for a question about lift and drag.

The tunnel is useful because the question is specific. It would be a poor model of the in-flight entertainment system.
Discovering the Question with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Turn a Topic into a Question

Ask the AI to make a simulation question.

Topic: the effect of a supply disruption on a product's price.
Turn it into three simulation questions. For each, name the system
boundary, the time horizon and the output that would answer it.

A good answer will name a comparison, not just a topic.

Exploration 2: Choose the Simplification

Ask what to leave out.

A simulation of a queue needs to answer: how long do customers wait when
one server is added? List what you would model and what you would leave
out. Justify each omission.

The omissions are the assumptions.

Exploration 3: Find the Assumption

Ask which assumption matters most.

Here is the simulation brief:
[paste it]

List the assumptions. Which one, if wrong, would change the answer most?
How would you test it?

The sensitive assumption is the next experiment.
Write a brief for one SimLab simulator. Name the question, the output and one assumption.
A simulation without a question is a toy. A simulation with a question is an argument you can test.

Exercise 1.1 (Level 1). Explain why a simulation is a question.

Exercise 1.2 (Level 2). Turn a topic into a simulation question.

Exercise 1.3 (Level 3). Name what to leave out and why.

Exercise 1.4 (Level 4). Find the most sensitive assumption.

Exercise 1.5 (Level 5). Write a complete brief for a real system.

• A simulation is a model with time.
  • The question comes before the tool.
  • A brief names the system, rules, horizon and output.
  • Every simulation is a simplification.
  • The sensitive assumption is the next experiment.

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Wrote a question
  • [ ] Named the boundary
  • [ ] Chose the output
  • [ ] Named one omission
  • [ ] Found one sensitive assumption

1. Which question was hardest to make specific?
  2. What did you leave out?
  3. Which assumption would you test first?
The question is set. The next chapter shows the shape every SimLab simulator shares.
Every simulator is a class with parameters, a run method and a seed.

SimLab simulators share a consistent interface:

  • a class that inherits from BaseSimulation
  • validated parameters
  • a run_simulation() method
  • a reset() method
  • get_parameters_info()
  • a random_seed for stochastic runs

A registry maps names to classes, so you can create a simulator without importing the class directly:

from sim_lab.core import SimulatorRegistry

sim = SimulatorRegistry.create("GameOfLife", pattern="glider", grid_size=(30, 30), days=60)
cells = sim.run_simulation()

The common shape makes the models comparable. You can learn one interface and explore many paradigms.

The interface does not make the models equivalent. A stock-market simulation and a forest-fire model answer different questions.

Model railways use standard gauge. Any compatible train can run on the track.

The gauge does not make every train the same. It makes them interoperable.

SimLab's interface is the gauge.
Discovering the Shape with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Read the Interface

Ask the AI to map a simulator to the base shape.

Here is a SimLab simulator class:
[paste it]

Identify its parameters, its state, its run method and its use of
random_seed. Explain what the base class provides and what the simulator
adds.

A good answer separates the shared plumbing from the model.

Exploration 2: Use the Registry

Ask how to create a simulator by name.

List the SimLab simulators and show how the registry creates one by name.
Explain one advantage and one risk of dynamic creation.

The risk is a typo or an unknown name; the advantage is discovery.

Exploration 3: Test the Parameters

Ask what validation should catch.

A simulator takes days, volatility and random_seed. List the invalid
values that should be rejected before the run and the error message a
student should see.

Validation is part of the teaching.

A simulator record:

Field Entry
Name StockMarketSimulation
Parameters start price, days, volatility, drift, event
State prices
Run run_simulation()
Seed random_seed
Output list of prices
Validation positive days, sensible volatility
Create one simulator through the registry. Print its parameters. Run it twice with the same seed and compare.
The common interface lets a class explore several paradigms without relearning the plumbing. The differences then become the lesson.

Exercise 2.1 (Level 1). List the shared interface methods.

Exercise 2.2 (Level 2). Create a simulator through the registry.

Exercise 2.3 (Level 3). Identify the parameters and state.

Exercise 2.4 (Level 4). Test one invalid parameter.

Exercise 2.5 (Level 5). Compare two simulators that share the interface but model different systems.

• Every simulator shares a class, parameters, run method and seed.
  • The registry creates simulators by name.
  • The interface makes models comparable, not equivalent.
  • Validation is part of the teaching.
  • The differences between models are the lesson.

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Read the interface
  • [ ] Created a simulator by name
  • [ ] Named the parameters
  • [ ] Tested one invalid value
  • [ ] Compared two models

1. Which parameter mattered most?
  2. What did the registry hide?
  3. What did the shared shape make easier?
The shape is clear. The next chapter changes how time advances.
The paradigm is often a decision about how time moves.

Two common ways to advance time:

  • Discrete time: the simulation moves in fixed steps. Each step updates the state. Stock prices, resource levels and product demand often work this way.
  • Discrete event: the simulation jumps from one scheduled event to the next. The state changes only when something happens. Queues and service systems often work this way.

A discrete-time model is easy to explain and easy to plot. It can waste computation on quiet periods.

A discrete-event model is efficient when events are sparse. It can be harder to explain because there is no fixed clock.

The choice changes what you can see. A daily price model hides intraday shocks. An event model can represent them.
A calendar with daily boxes is discrete time. A calendar with appointments is discrete event. Both represent a week; they answer different questions.

Exploration 1: Choose the Clock

Ask the AI to choose a paradigm.

A simulation needs to answer: how does a queue grow when arrivals double?
Should time advance in fixed steps or jump between events? Explain the
trade-off and the output you would plot.

A queue is usually a discrete-event problem.

Exploration 2: Find the Event

Ask what counts as an event.

In a queueing simulation, list the events, the state they change and the
order in which they can occur. Include arrival, start service, finish
service and abandonment.

The event list is the model.

Exploration 3: Compare the Outputs

Ask what each paradigm shows.

Compare a daily discrete-time model of a queue with a discrete-event
model. What does each make visible or hide? Which would you use for a
staffing decision?

The answer depends on the question.

A time model record:

Field Entry
Paradigm Discrete event
Events Arrival, start service, finish
State Queue length, servers busy
Clock Event time
Output Wait time, utilisation
Risk Missing abandonment
Run one discrete-time and one discrete-event simulator. Plot the output and explain what each makes visible.
Time is a good first comparison because students can see the difference in the output. The paradigm is not abstract; it changes what the graph shows.

Exercise 3.1 (Level 1). Explain discrete time and discrete event.

Exercise 3.2 (Level 2). List the events in a queue.

Exercise 3.3 (Level 3). Run both paradigms and compare the plots.

Exercise 3.4 (Level 4). Choose a paradigm for a staffing decision.

Exercise 3.5 (Level 5). Design a model that captures one intraday shock a daily model would hide.

• Discrete time moves in fixed steps.
  • Discrete event jumps between scheduled events.
  • The choice changes what the model can see.
  • A queue is usually an event model.
  • The question decides the clock.

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Explained both paradigms
  • [ ] Listed the events
  • [ ] Ran both
  • [ ] Compared the plots
  • [ ] Chose one for a decision

1. Which clock was easier to reason about?
  2. What did the daily model hide?
  3. Which output convinced you?
Time is chosen. The next chapter adds randomness.
A random simulation is an experiment. The seed is part of the method.

Many simulations use randomness: stock returns, arrivals, infection events, agent choices.

A random result on its own is an anecdote. A reproducible result is evidence. The random_seed fixes the sequence so another person can rerun the model and get the same output.

Randomness also needs a distribution. "Random" is not enough. Are arrivals Poisson? Are returns normal? Are agent choices uniform? The distribution is an assumption.

Three common families:

  • Monte Carlo: sample many times to estimate a number.
  • Markov chain: move between states with probabilities.
  • Gillespie SSA: simulate individual stochastic events in continuous time.

A dice game is fair if the dice are fair and the rules are clear. Rolling once tells you little. Rolling many times tells you the distribution.

The seed is the record of which rolls you made. The distribution is the claim about the dice.

Exploration 1: Find the Distribution

Ask what randomness the model assumes.

Here is a simulator and its parameters:
[paste it]

Identify every random process. For each, name the distribution, the
parameter and the assumption. What would change if the distribution were
wrong?

A good answer will not accept "random" as a description.

Exploration 2: Test the Seed

Ask how to prove reproducibility.

Run the same simulation twice with the same random_seed and once with a
different seed. Explain what should be identical and what should change.
Design the evidence you would record.

The same seed should reproduce the run; the different seed should show variation.

Exploration 3: Estimate with Monte Carlo

Ask how many samples are enough.

A Monte Carlo estimate has a standard error. Explain how the error
changes with sample size and how you would report the estimate with an
uncertainty range.

The answer is a confidence interval, not a single number.

A randomness record:

Field Entry
Process Daily return
Distribution Normal
Parameters Mean, standard deviation
Seed 42
Samples 1000
Estimate Mean and interval
Assumption Independence
Run a Monte Carlo estimator with 100, 1000 and 10000 samples. Report the estimate and the uncertainty. Repeat with the same seed.
Reproducibility is an assessment criterion. A student who reports a seed and a validation is more credible than one who reports a single lucky run.

Exercise 4.1 (Level 1). Explain why a seed matters.

Exercise 4.2 (Level 2). Identify the random process in a simulator.

Exercise 4.3 (Level 3). Reproduce a run with the same seed.

Exercise 4.4 (Level 4). Report a Monte Carlo estimate with uncertainty.

Exercise 4.5 (Level 5). Compare two distributions on the same question.

• Randomness needs a distribution, not just a label.
  • The seed makes a run reproducible.
  • Monte Carlo estimates need uncertainty.
  • Markov and Gillespie models have different time assumptions.
  • Reproducibility is part of the evidence.

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Found the random process
  • [ ] Named the distribution
  • [ ] Reproduced a run
  • [ ] Reported uncertainty
  • [ ] Tested a second seed

1. Which assumption was hidden in "random"?
  2. What did the second seed change?
  3. How many samples were enough?
Randomness is controlled. The next chapter looks at emergence in cells and agents.
Some behaviour is not in the rules. It appears when the rules interact.

Cellular automata update a grid of cells with local rules. Each cell looks at its neighbours and changes state. Game of Life and forest-fire models are examples.

Agent-based models give each agent its own state and rules. Agents interact, move or adapt. Boids and simple market models are examples.

Both produce emergence: patterns at the system level that no single rule contains. A traffic jam, a flock or a forest fire can emerge from simple local behaviour.

Emergence is powerful and easy to overinterpret. A pattern in the output is a result of the model, not proof about the world.

No bird has a plan for the flock. Each bird follows a few rules: avoid collision, match direction, stay close.

The flock is what the rules look like at scale.

Exploration 1: Separate the Rules from the Pattern

Ask the AI to describe both.

Here is a cellular automaton or agent model:
[paste it]

List the local rules and the global pattern. Explain why the pattern is
not contained in any single rule. Mark what the model does not prove
about the real system.

A good answer will keep the model and the world apart.

Exploration 2: Change One Rule

Ask what happens.

Change one rule in the model, such as the infection probability or the
separation distance. Predict the effect, then test it. Explain whether
the result matched the prediction.

The experiment is the lesson.

Exploration 3: Find the Validation

Ask how to check the pattern.

The model produces a familiar-looking pattern. What would you compare it
with to validate the model? Name one qualitative and one quantitative
check.

A familiar pattern is not validation.

An emergence record:

Field Entry
Model Forest fire
Local rule Tree ignites if a neighbour burns
Global pattern Clusters and criticality
Parameter Density, spread probability
Validation Known qualitative behaviour
Limitation Not a prediction for a specific forest
Run one cellular and one agent model. Change one parameter. Predict, test and explain.
Emergence is engaging and easy to demonstrate. The assessment should ask what the pattern does and does not establish.

Exercise 5.1 (Level 1). Explain emergence.

Exercise 5.2 (Level 2). Separate local rules from global pattern.

Exercise 5.3 (Level 3). Change one parameter and predict the effect.

Exercise 5.4 (Level 4). Validate a pattern qualitatively and quantitatively.

Exercise 5.5 (Level 5). Explain why a realistic-looking pattern is not proof.

• Cellular and agent models use local rules.
  • Global patterns can emerge from local interaction.
  • Emergence is a property of the model.
  • A familiar pattern is not validation.
  • Change one rule at a time.

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Named the local rules
  • [ ] Described the global pattern
  • [ ] Changed one parameter
  • [ ] Validated the pattern
  • [ ] Stated a limitation

1. Which pattern surprised you?
  2. Did the prediction match?
  3. What would count as validation?
Cells and agents are local. The next chapter adds feedback and networks.
A system with feedback can turn a small change into a large one.

System dynamics models stocks, flows and feedback loops. A stock accumulates; a flow changes it; a feedback loop connects the state back to the flow.

A reinforcing loop amplifies. A balancing loop stabilises. The same system can contain both.

Network models put processes on a graph. The structure of the network changes the result: a disease spreads differently on a grid, a random graph or a hub-and-spoke network.

Domain models apply these ideas: predator-prey, epidemics and supply chains.

The teaching point is that structure matters. A model with the same average behaviour but a different network can produce a different outcome.

A thermostat is a balancing loop. The room cools, the sensor notices, the heater turns on, the room warms, the heater turns off.

A broken thermostat is a reinforcing loop with no brake.

Exploration 1: Find the Loop

Ask the AI to identify the feedback.

Here is a system dynamics or domain model:
[paste it]

Identify the stocks, flows and feedback loops. Mark each loop as
reinforcing or balancing. Explain what would happen if the loop were
removed.

A good answer will name the mechanism, not just the shape.

Exploration 2: Change the Network

Ask how structure changes the result.

The same epidemic model runs on a grid, a random graph and a hub-and-spoke
network. Predict how the peak and the spread change. Explain why.

The network is part of the model.

Exploration 3: Validate the Domain Model

Ask what theory predicts.

A predator-prey model should produce closed orbits around an equilibrium.
Explain how you would check that against the analytic result and what a
numerical simulation might get wrong.

Validation is a comparison, not a vibe.

A structure record:

Model Structure Validation
Predator-prey Two populations, interaction Orbits around equilibrium
SIR Susceptible, infected, recovered Peak rises with R0
Supply chain Multi-tier inventory Bullwhip effect
Network Graph topology Spread depends on structure
Run one system-dynamics model and one network or domain model. Change one structural parameter. Explain the result.
Feedback and networks teach that the same local rules can produce different system behaviour. The assessment should ask which structure produced the result.

Exercise 6.1 (Level 1). Explain a reinforcing and a balancing loop.

Exercise 6.2 (Level 2). Identify stocks and flows.

Exercise 6.3 (Level 3). Change a network and predict the effect.

Exercise 6.4 (Level 4). Validate a domain model against theory.

Exercise 6.5 (Level 5). Explain why structure matters more than an average rate.

• System dynamics models stocks, flows and feedback.
  • Reinforcing loops amplify; balancing loops stabilise.
  • Network structure changes the outcome.
  • Domain models need validation against theory.
  • Structure is part of the explanation.

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Found a feedback loop
  • [ ] Named its type
  • [ ] Changed a network
  • [ ] Validated a domain model
  • [ ] Explained the structure

1. Which loop mattered most?
  2. How did the network change the result?
  3. What did theory predict?
The structure is modelled. The final chapter validates, reproduces and teaches.
A simulation result is evidence only when someone else can reproduce it and check it against something.

Three questions decide whether a simulation result is useful:

  • Reproducible: can another person rerun it and get the same output?
  • Validated: does it match a known analytic result, a qualitative law or a measured pattern?
  • Interpreted: does it answer the question, and what does it not prove?

A seed is necessary but not sufficient. A model can be perfectly reproducible and still wrong.

Validation examples:

  • queueing: utilisation and queue length trends
  • Lotka-Volterra: closed orbits around equilibrium
  • exponential decay: matches the analytic curve in expectation
  • Monte Carlo pi: converges as samples grow
  • SIR: peak rises with R0, herd-immunity threshold
A lab report states the method, the result, the comparison with theory and the uncertainty. A result without a comparison is a number, not a finding.

Exploration 1: Choose the Check

Ask the AI to validate a model.

Here is a simulation result and the model:
[paste them]

Propose one analytic check, one qualitative check and one sensitivity
test. Explain what each would prove and what it would miss.

A good answer will not rely on a single check.

Exploration 2: Read the Uncertainty

Ask what the random variation means.

The result changes between seeds. Explain how to report the estimate
with uncertainty and how many runs you would use. Do not report a single
run as the answer.

The distribution of runs is the evidence.

Exploration 3: Design the Assessment

Ask how to grade the project.

Design a rubric for a simulation project. Reward reproducibility,
validation, interpretation and code quality. Do not reward the number of
plots.

The rubric is the teaching contract.

An assessment rubric:

Criterion Evidence
Reproducibility Seed set, report, rerun identical
Validation Comparison with theory or data
Analysis Interpretation of the result
Code quality Parameterised, readable, uses the API
Take one simulation. Record the seed, the output, the validation and the interpretation. Ask a peer to rerun it.
Assessment should reward the reasoning, not the visual polish. A short notebook that validates and interprets one result beats ten plots with no commentary.

Exercise 7.1 (Level 1). Name the three questions.

Exercise 7.2 (Level 2). Record a seed and rerun a model.

Exercise 7.3 (Level 3). Validate against one analytic result.

Exercise 7.4 (Level 4). Report uncertainty across runs.

Exercise 7.5 (Level 5). Write a rubric for a simulation project.

• A result needs reproducibility, validation and interpretation.
  • A seed is necessary but not sufficient.
  • Compare with theory, a qualitative law or data.
  • Report uncertainty across runs.
  • Assess reasoning, not plot count.

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Recorded a seed
  • [ ] Reran the model
  • [ ] Validated one result
  • [ ] Reported uncertainty
  • [ ] Wrote a rubric

1. Which validation was strongest?
  2. What did the seed not prove?
  3. What would you change in the assessment?
The practice is complete. The SimLab docs list every simulator and its parameters.

questions.explanation: A simulation without a question is a toy. The question decides the model, the horizon and the output.

options: Discrete time moves in fixed steps; discrete event jumps between scheduled events
Discrete time is random; discrete event is deterministic
questions.explanation: The paradigm is often a decision about how time advances.

options: To make the run reproducible for another person
To make the model more accurate
